claims.text: The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen produces representative defect microstructures in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
A machine-learning model can explicitly integrate defect scattering and oxygen-impurity effects into transport simulations.
Quantum and defect scattering dominate transport in the approximately 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering involving oxygen-induced defects dominates transport in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr induces defects and local structural distortions.
Oxygen-induced defects and local structural distortions alter electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced defects and local structural distortions alter phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Perfect-crystal analytical models omit relevant defect- and oxygen-related scattering mechanisms.
Training on experimental data containing defect and oxygen effects allows the machine-learning model to adjust for scattering mechanisms absent from perfect-crystal models.
Including defect and oxygen effects will improve predictions of both thermal and electrical conductivity relative to conventional defect-free analytical models.
The proposed approach will reduce average thermal- and electrical-conductivity prediction error by at least approximately 10–20% relative to conventional defect-free models.
Ideal, defect-free conductivity models typically exhibit larger discrepancies against measurements from defect-bearing, oxygen-containing samples.
The hypothesis is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content near 1 wt.% over approximately 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Applicability outside the stated temperature regimes or at substantially different oxygen levels is uncertain.
